questions.q: What is the primary narrative function of the first stanza in *Phool Kee*?
questions.a: The first stanza serves as **exposition**: it introduces the protagonist (the separated woman), her situation (husband gone to a distant land), and her core emotion (longing). A wrong answer like “it describes the night” reveals the student is confusing stanza 1 with stanza 2 — they haven’t distinguished the *setup* from the *intensification*.

questions.q: Explain in your own words how the narrative shifts from stanza 1 to stanza 2. What changes in the woman’s emotional state?
questions.a: Stanza 1 is **static waiting** (“I have been watching the path since birth”); stanza 2 becomes **active suffering** — night deepens, wind howls, the moon loses beauty, and she admits “I have not found peace.” A wrong answer that says “both stanzas show sadness” misses the structural shift from *passive waiting* to *active, sensory anguish* — the narrative complication.

questions.q: Identify the exact phrase in stanza 3 that marks the **climax** of the narrative arc and justify why it is the turning point.
questions.a: The phrase **“dj nsb >k¡ib dku” (extinguish the lamp, O lamp)** — actually a plea *not* to let the lamp go out — is the climax. The woman moves from describing pain to **direct action**: she commands the lamp to survive so her husband can find his way. A wrong answer picking “ewfn jg, nq u;ku” (stay awake, don’t sleep) shows they see only desperation, not the *agency* that marks the narrative peak.

questions.q: Compare the narrative role of the **lamp (dkuu)** in stanza 3 with the **path (Hkou)** in stanza 1. How does the shift from path to lamp restructure the story?
questions.a: The **path** in stanza 1 is a *passive symbol* of hope (she watches it). The **lamp** in stanza 3 becomes an *active agent* she addresses and commands. This shifts the narrative from **external waiting** to **internal agency** — she now participates in the resolution. A wrong answer treating both as mere “symbols of hope” misses the structural promotion of the lamp to a character she bargains with.

questions.q: Evaluate whether the three-stanza structure effectively resolves the narrative tension. Support your judgment with evidence from the text.
questions.a: **Yes, partially.** The prayer to the lamp (“stay lit so he returns”) provides emotional closure — she transforms despair into ritual. But the husband’s return is **not shown**; the narrative ends on *anticipation*, not fulfillment. A wrong answer claiming “complete resolution” ignores the open ending; one saying “no resolution” misses the psychological closure of the prayer act.

questions.q: Write a fourth stanza (4-6 lines in Hindi) that continues the narrative *after* the lamp prayer, maintaining the same voice, imagery, and structural logic.
questions.a: A strong stanza will: (a) use Braj-inflected vocabulary (*eèkqiqj, xksoqQy, fiz;rek*), (b) show the lamp’s response (flaring steady / flickering), (c) introduce a sensory sign of return (footsteps, dust on road), and (d) end on a note of *quiet hope* not full reunion. A weak answer jumps to “he came back” — breaking the poem’s restraint — or switches to modern Hindi, losing the linguistic texture.
